course.title: African American History
course.description: A careful survey of African American history, from West African origins and the transatlantic slave trade through slavery, emancipation, Reconstruction, the Great Migration, the Civil Rights Movement, and the present day. The course follows four centuries of endurance, resistance, achievement, and cultural contribution with accurate dates and respect for the people involved. Structure and reference material adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: The first documented enslaved Africans arrived in English North America, at Point Comfort in Virginia, in what year?
questions.explanation: In August 1619 the ship White Lion brought about twenty enslaved Africans to Virginia, the first documented arrival in the English colonies.

questions.prompt: The forced ocean voyage that carried captive Africans to the Americas is known as the...
questions.explanation: The Middle Passage was the brutal middle leg of the triangular trade, crossing the Atlantic in horrific conditions.

questions.prompt: Which man escaped slavery and became one of the most influential abolitionist writers and orators of the 1800s?
questions.explanation: Frederick Douglass escaped bondage in 1838 and became a famed speaker, author, and newspaper publisher.

questions.prompt: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect in what year?
questions.explanation: President Lincoln issued it January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in Confederate-held territory to be free.

questions.prompt: Which 1954 Supreme Court case declared segregated public schools unconstitutional?
questions.explanation: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned the 'separate but equal' doctrine in public education.

questions.prompt: The Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955-1956 began after the arrest of...
questions.explanation: Rosa Parks was arrested December 1, 1955, for refusing to give up her bus seat, sparking the yearlong boycott.

questions.prompt: Which musical genre originated in the 1970s Bronx?
questions.explanation: Hip-hop emerged in the Bronx in the early 1970s; jazz, blues, and gospel are older forms rooted earlier in the century and before.

questions.prompt: Barack Obama was elected the first Black president of the United States in...
questions.explanation: Obama won the presidency in November 2008 and took office in January 2009.

lessons.title: West African origins and the transatlantic slave trade
lessons.grammar_note: Prefer 'enslaved people' over 'slaves' - it names the condition done to people rather than defining them by it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to describe the West African societies from which many captive Africans came, explain how the transatlantic slave trade operated across three continents, and state the human scale of the Middle Passage. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in what year did the first documented enslaved Africans reach the English colonies, and what was the name of the sea crossing that brought them? Keep those two facts in mind, because this lesson explains what came before that 1619 arrival. The people forced onto those ships were not a blank beginning; they carried languages, religions, crafts, farming knowledge, and political traditions that would survive the crossing and reshape the Americas.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Long before European contact, West Africa held powerful, organized states. The empires of Ghana, Mali, and Songhai grew rich on trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt. Mali's ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca around 1324, and Timbuktu became a center of scholarship. From the 1440s Portuguese traders began buying captives along the coast, and after 1500 the trade expanded enormously to supply plantation labor in the Americas. The transatlantic trade ran as a triangle: manufactured goods from Europe to Africa, enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas, and sugar, tobacco, and cotton back to Europe. Over roughly three and a half centuries about 12.5 million Africans were loaded onto ships, and historians estimate close to 10.7 million survived the crossing, with the rest dying at sea during the Middle Passage.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: The trans-Saharan trade and the West African empires of Ghana, Mali, and Songhai flourished between roughly the 700s and the 1500s. Portugal opened sustained Atlantic trading in enslaved people in the 1440s. The trade peaked in the 1700s, when Britain, Portugal, France, and others shipped hundreds of thousands of people per decade. The first documented enslaved Africans in English North America arrived in August 1619 at Point Comfort, Virginia, aboard the White Lion. The Kingdom of Kongo, the Asante, the Dahomey, and the Oyo were among the African states entangled in the trade, sometimes as suppliers of captives taken in war. The Middle Passage itself, often six to ten weeks long, became a byword for cruelty: people were chained below decks in spaces too small to stand, and disease, dehydration, and despair killed many.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three great West African empires mentioned here. 2) Roughly how many Africans were forced onto slave ships across the whole trade? 3) What were the three legs of the triangular trade? 4) In what decade did Portuguese traders begin sustained purchases of captives along the African coast? 5) About how long could the Middle Passage last? Answers: 1) Ghana, Mali, and Songhai. 2) About 12.5 million were loaded, and roughly 10.7 million survived the crossing. 3) Goods from Europe to Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, and raw commodities like sugar and tobacco back to Europe. 4) The 1440s. 5) Roughly six to ten weeks, depending on the route and weather.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining the people who were enslaved as having no history before capture; West Africa held wealthy empires, universities, and complex trade long before the Atlantic trade. Mistake: assuming the trade was small; the roughly 12.5 million people moved make it one of the largest forced migrations in human history. Mistake: treating 1619 as the start of the whole Atlantic trade; it marks the first documented arrival in the English colonies only, decades into a trade already supplying Spanish and Portuguese colonies. Exit ticket: (a) What year marks the first documented enslaved Africans in English North America? (b) What is the Middle Passage? Answers: 1619; the forced, deadly ocean crossing that carried captive Africans from Africa to the Americas.

lessons.title: Slavery in colonial and antebellum America
lessons.grammar_note: 'Antebellum' means 'before the war' - here it refers to the period before the U.S. Civil War, roughly 1815 to 1861.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain how slavery took legal root in the American colonies, how the cotton economy made it central to the nation's wealth, and how the domestic slave trade tore families apart in the decades before the Civil War. Warm-up: from the last lesson, about how many Africans survived the Middle Passage, and what crop would come to dominate the slave economy of the Deep South? This lesson follows enslaved people from the tobacco fields of the colonial Chesapeake to the cotton plantations that spread across the South after 1800, and it shows how law and economics hardened slavery into a permanent, inherited, race-based condition.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In the 1600s, Virginia and Maryland gradually wrote slavery into law, making it lifelong and hereditary and tying it to African ancestry. A 1662 Virginia law decreed that a child's status followed the mother, ensuring that enslavement passed down generations. At the nation's founding the Constitution of 1787 counted an enslaved person as three-fifths of a free person for representation and allowed the slave trade to continue until 1808. Eli Whitney's cotton gin, patented in 1793, made short-staple cotton enormously profitable and drove slavery's expansion westward. Though importing enslaved people became illegal in 1808, a vast domestic trade grew instead, moving roughly a million people from the Upper South to the cotton frontier of the Deep South. Enslaved people endured forced labor, violence, and the constant threat of sale, yet built families, churches, music, and community under these conditions.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: The 1662 Virginia law fixing status through the mother; the 1705 Virginia slave codes that further stripped rights; the Three-Fifths Compromise of 1787; the cotton gin of 1793; and the Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves, effective January 1, 1808. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 tried to balance slave and free states. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 forced Northerners to help capture escapees. The Dred Scott decision of 1857 ruled that Black people, enslaved or free, could not be citizens and had no standing to sue. By 1860 nearly four million people were enslaved in the United States, the overwhelming majority in the South, where cotton had become the country's leading export.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What did the 1662 Virginia law establish about the status of children? 2) What invention of 1793 expanded cotton slavery? 3) When did the legal importation of enslaved people into the United States end? 4) What did the Dred Scott decision of 1857 rule? 5) About how many people were enslaved in the United States by 1860? Answers: 1) A child inherited the enslaved or free status of the mother. 2) Eli Whitney's cotton gin. 3) January 1, 1808, though a large domestic trade continued. 4) That Black people were not citizens and could not sue in federal court. 5) Nearly four million.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the 1808 ban ended the buying and selling of people; instead a brutal internal trade moved roughly a million people south and west. Mistake: assuming slavery was mainly a Deep South phenomenon from the start; it was legal in all thirteen colonies and only gradually abolished in the North. Mistake: picturing enslaved people as passive; they resisted through work slowdowns, escape, preserving culture, and open rebellion, which the next lesson covers. Exit ticket: (a) What crop and machine drove slavery's westward spread after 1793? (b) What did the Three-Fifths Compromise do? Answers: cotton and the cotton gin; it counted each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for deciding a state's representation in Congress.

lessons.title: Resistance and abolition
lessons.grammar_note: The 'Underground Railroad' was neither underground nor a railroad - it was a secret network of people and safe houses, named with railroad code words.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe the many forms resistance to slavery took, from daily acts to armed revolt, and identify the leading figures of the abolition movement and the Underground Railroad. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, who escaped slavery to become a renowned abolitionist writer and orator? That person, Frederick Douglass, is one of several leaders this lesson introduces. Resistance was constant wherever slavery existed, and a growing movement of Black and white abolitionists worked, by word and by action, to end it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Enslaved people resisted in countless ways: breaking tools, feigning illness, preserving African traditions, escaping, and sometimes rising in revolt. Open rebellions, though rare and almost always crushed, terrified slaveholders. Meanwhile a northern abolition movement grew through the 1830s, led by figures Black and white who argued that slavery was a moral evil. The Underground Railroad was a secret network of free Black communities, formerly enslaved people, Quakers, and other allies who sheltered and guided escapees north toward free states and Canada. It was dangerous work: helpers and escapees alike faced prison or death, and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made the north unsafe too. The movement's newspapers, speeches, and narratives, including Douglass's autobiography, turned personal testimony into a powerful political force.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Gabriel's planned rebellion near Richmond in 1800 and the Denmark Vesey conspiracy in Charleston in 1822 were both discovered and suppressed. Nat Turner led an armed uprising in Southampton County, Virginia, in 1831, after which laws tightened sharply. William Lloyd Garrison launched the abolitionist newspaper The Liberator in 1831. Frederick Douglass, born into slavery around 1818, escaped in 1838, published his Narrative in 1845, and founded the newspaper The North Star in 1847. Harriet Tubman, who escaped around 1849, returned repeatedly to lead roughly seventy people to freedom on the Underground Railroad and later served the Union as a scout and spy. Sojourner Truth became a powerful voice for abolition and women's rights, and John Brown's 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry pushed the nation closer to war.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who led the 1831 armed uprising in Southampton County, Virginia? 2) What was the Underground Railroad? 3) Name the newspaper Frederick Douglass founded in 1847. 4) Who is known for returning to the South many times to guide enslaved people to freedom? 5) What did the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 require? Answers: 1) Nat Turner. 2) A secret network of people and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape to free states and Canada. 3) The North Star. 4) Harriet Tubman. 5) It compelled citizens, including Northerners, to help capture and return escaped enslaved people.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining the Underground Railroad as an actual railway; it was a human network using railroad terms as code, with 'conductors' and 'stations.' Mistake: assuming abolition was purely a white movement; free and formerly enslaved Black people were its backbone, as writers, organizers, and conductors. Mistake: thinking enslaved people accepted their condition; resistance was everywhere, from subtle sabotage to open revolt. Exit ticket: (a) Name two leaders of resistance or abolition from this lesson. (b) Why was helping on the Underground Railroad so dangerous after 1850? Answers: any two of Nat Turner, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth, William Lloyd Garrison, John Brown; because the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made aiding escapees a federal crime, with heavy penalties even in free states.

questions.prompt: Over the entire transatlantic trade, roughly how many Africans were forced onto slave ships?
questions.explanation: Historians estimate about 12.5 million people were embarked, with roughly 10.7 million surviving the Middle Passage.

questions.prompt: The 1793 invention that made short-staple cotton highly profitable and expanded slavery was the...
questions.explanation: Eli Whitney's cotton gin quickly separated seeds from cotton fiber, fueling the plantation economy's spread westward.

questions.prompt: The legal importation of enslaved people into the United States ended, by federal law, in...
questions.explanation: The Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves took effect January 1, 1808, though a large internal slave trade continued.

questions.prompt: Harriet Tubman is best known for her work with the...
questions.explanation: After escaping slavery, Tubman returned repeatedly to lead enslaved people to freedom along the Underground Railroad.

questions.prompt: Nat Turner led an armed uprising of enslaved people in Virginia in...
questions.explanation: Turner's 1831 rebellion in Southampton County led Southern states to pass harsher slave codes.

questions.prompt: Frederick Douglass published his famous autobiography, the Narrative, in...
questions.explanation: The Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass appeared in 1845 and became a landmark abolitionist text.

lessons.title: Civil War, emancipation, and the collapse of Reconstruction
lessons.grammar_note: 'Reconstruction' (capital R) names the specific 1865-1877 period of rebuilding and civil-rights expansion after the Civil War, not reconstruction in general.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain how the Civil War ended slavery, what rights the Reconstruction amendments granted, and how white backlash dismantled those gains and built the Jim Crow system of segregation. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, in what year did the Emancipation Proclamation take effect? That 1863 order was a turning point, but freedom on paper and freedom in practice proved to be two different struggles. This lesson covers one of the most hopeful and then one of the most bitter chapters in the story.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Civil War (1861-1865) grew directly out of the conflict over slavery. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of January 1, 1863, declared enslaved people in Confederate territory free and allowed Black men to enlist; nearly 180,000 served in the United States Colored Troops. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, abolished slavery nationwide. During Reconstruction (1865-1877), the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) granted citizenship and equal protection, and the Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote based on race. Black men voted and held office in large numbers. But the disputed election of 1876, settled by the Compromise of 1877, withdrew federal troops from the South. White Democrats regained control, and over the next decades they imposed Jim Crow laws, segregation, and devices like poll taxes and literacy tests that stripped most Black Southerners of the vote.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: The Emancipation Proclamation of January 1, 1863; the service of the 54th Massachusetts Infantry and the broader United States Colored Troops; the Thirteenth Amendment of 1865; and the creation of the Freedmen's Bureau in 1865 to aid formerly enslaved people. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) and Fifteenth Amendment (1870) secured citizenship and voting rights. Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche K. Bruce became the first Black U.S. senators in the 1870s. The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction. The Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson decision in 1896 upheld 'separate but equal,' giving legal cover to segregation. Ida B. Wells documented and campaigned against lynching in the 1890s, exposing the violence that enforced the new racial order.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What did the Thirteenth Amendment do, and when was it ratified? 2) Which two Reconstruction amendments granted citizenship and voting rights? 3) What agency was created in 1865 to help formerly enslaved people? 4) What ended Reconstruction? 5) What doctrine did Plessy v. Ferguson uphold in 1896? Answers: 1) It abolished slavery throughout the United States, ratified December 1865. 2) The Fourteenth (1868, citizenship and equal protection) and the Fifteenth (1870, voting rights). 3) The Freedmen's Bureau. 4) The Compromise of 1877, which withdrew federal troops from the South. 5) 'Separate but equal,' which legalized racial segregation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the Emancipation Proclamation freed everyone immediately; it applied to Confederate-held areas, and full legal abolition came with the Thirteenth Amendment in December 1865. Mistake: treating Reconstruction as a failure of Black leadership; it was ended by organized white violence and the federal government's retreat. Mistake: assuming segregation was always informal; Jim Crow was an explicit legal system backed by the courts after 1896. Exit ticket: (a) What did the Fifteenth Amendment guarantee? (b) What was Jim Crow? Answers: that the right to vote could not be denied on account of race; a system of state and local laws that enforced racial segregation and disenfranchisement across the South.

lessons.title: The Great Migration and the Harlem Renaissance
lessons.grammar_note: Capitalize 'Great Migration' and 'Harlem Renaissance' - both are proper names for specific historical movements, not general descriptions.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe why millions of Black Americans left the rural South in the twentieth century, where they went, and how this movement fueled an explosion of art, music, and writing centered in Harlem. Warm-up: recall from the last lesson what Jim Crow laws and lynching did to life in the South. Those conditions, along with the promise of jobs in northern industry, set millions of people in motion. This lesson follows that journey and the cultural flowering it helped produce.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Great Migration was the movement of roughly six million Black Americans out of the rural South to cities in the North, Midwest, and West between about 1916 and 1970. People fled Jim Crow, violence, and poverty, and sought factory jobs opened up by the two world wars. Cities like Chicago, Detroit, New York, and Philadelphia saw their Black populations surge. In the 1920s, the Harlem neighborhood of New York became the heart of a cultural movement, the Harlem Renaissance, in which Black writers, musicians, and artists produced work of lasting power and asserted a confident, modern Black identity. Organizations like the NAACP, founded in 1909, and Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association built political and economic movements, while the migration reshaped American cities for good.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: The NAACP was founded in 1909, and W. E. B. Du Bois edited its magazine, The Crisis. The Great Migration's first wave ran from about 1916 through the 1930s, a second from the 1940s into the 1970s. Marcus Garvey led a mass Black-nationalist movement in the early 1920s. The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s and early 1930s produced poets and writers such as Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, and Countee Cullen. In music, Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong brought jazz to national prominence, and Bessie Smith reigned as a queen of the blues. Painter Aaron Douglas and sculptor Augusta Savage shaped its visual art. The movement declined with the Great Depression but permanently changed American culture.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) About how many people moved during the Great Migration, and over what rough span of years? 2) Name two cities whose Black populations grew sharply. 3) What neighborhood gave the Harlem Renaissance its name? 4) Name two writers of the Harlem Renaissance. 5) In what year was the NAACP founded? Answers: 1) Roughly six million people, from about 1916 to 1970. 2) Any two of Chicago, Detroit, New York, and Philadelphia. 3) Harlem, in New York City. 4) Any two of Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, and Countee Cullen. 5) 1909.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the Great Migration was a single short event; it unfolded in two long waves over more than half a century. Mistake: assuming the North was free of racism; migrants met segregation in housing, discrimination in hiring, and sometimes violence, though they gained the vote and new opportunities. Mistake: reducing the Harlem Renaissance to music alone; it spanned literature, painting, theater, and political thought. Exit ticket: (a) What two broad forces pushed and pulled people during the Great Migration? (b) What was the Harlem Renaissance? Answers: the push of Jim Crow, violence, and poverty, and the pull of northern industrial jobs; a 1920s flowering of Black literature, music, and art centered in Harlem that asserted a modern Black identity.

lessons.title: The Civil Rights Movement
lessons.grammar_note: 'Civil rights' are the basic legal rights to equal treatment and participation; the capitalized 'Civil Rights Movement' names the organized mid-century struggle to secure them.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to trace the major campaigns and victories of the Civil Rights Movement, name its key leaders, and identify the landmark laws of 1964 and 1965. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which 1954 Supreme Court case struck down segregated public schools, and whose 1955 arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott? Those two events open this lesson. The movement combined courtroom strategy, mass nonviolent protest, and extraordinary personal courage to dismantle the legal framework of Jim Crow.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The modern Civil Rights Movement sought to end legal segregation and secure voting rights through the courts, organized protest, and nonviolent direct action. The NAACP's legal campaign won Brown v. Board of Education in 1954, declaring school segregation unconstitutional. The Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955-1956 brought Martin Luther King Jr. to national attention and showed the power of collective nonviolent protest. Through the late 1950s and 1960s, sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and marches met fierce resistance, and the images of that resistance moved national opinion. The campaign crested with the 1963 March on Washington and King's 'I Have a Dream' speech, and then with two landmark laws: the Civil Rights Act of 1964, banning segregation and discrimination, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, protecting the ballot.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Brown v. Board of Education (1954); the murder of Emmett Till (1955); the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-1956), led by Martin Luther King Jr. and sparked by Rosa Parks; the Little Rock Nine integrating Central High School (1957); the Greensboro sit-ins (1960); the Freedom Rides (1961); the Birmingham campaign and the March on Washington (1963); the Civil Rights Act (1964); the Selma to Montgomery marches and the Voting Rights Act (1965). Leaders and organizers included King, Thurgood Marshall, John Lewis, Ella Baker, Fannie Lou Hamer, Bayard Rustin, Diane Nash, and many others. King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was assassinated in Memphis on April 4, 1968.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What did Brown v. Board of Education decide, and in what year? 2) Whose arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott? 3) At what 1963 event did King deliver the 'I Have a Dream' speech? 4) What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 do? 5) What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 protect? Answers: 1) That segregated public schools are unconstitutional, in 1954. 2) Rosa Parks, in December 1955. 3) The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. 4) It outlawed segregation in public places and banned discrimination in employment. 5) It protected the right to vote, banning practices like literacy tests used to disenfranchise Black voters.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking one leader drove the movement; it depended on thousands of organizers, local activists, students, and ordinary citizens who risked their lives. Mistake: assuming Brown instantly desegregated schools; enforcement dragged for years against fierce resistance. Mistake: confusing the two great laws; the 1964 Act targeted segregation and discrimination broadly, while the 1965 Act specifically protected voting. Exit ticket: (a) Name the two landmark federal laws of 1964 and 1965. (b) Why was nonviolent direct action, like sit-ins and marches, so effective? Answers: the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965; it exposed the brutality of segregation to a national audience and built moral pressure that forced political change.

lessons.title: Black Power, culture, achievement, and the ongoing story
lessons.grammar_note: Use 'hip-hop' with the hyphen for the broad culture and genre; the four elements are DJing, MCing (rapping), graffiti art, and breakdancing.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe the Black Power movement and the decades after the 1960s, name major Black contributions to music, literature, and science, and connect that long history to the present day. Warm-up: from the last lesson, which two federal laws of 1964 and 1965 ended legal segregation and protected voting? Those victories did not end the struggle for equality, and they coincided with a new assertion of Black pride, power, and cultural achievement. This capstone lesson ties the whole course together and brings the story into our own time.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: As the 1960s went on, many activists pressed beyond integration toward Black self-determination, economic power, and pride, a current known as Black Power. Malcolm X urged self-reliance and dignity before his assassination in 1965, and the Black Panther Party, founded in Oakland in 1966, combined community programs with militant self-defense. In the decades that followed, Black Americans won new political offices, broke barriers in every profession, and transformed world culture. Music runs through the whole story: blues and gospel grew from the rural South, jazz became a national art form, and hip-hop, born in the 1970s Bronx, became a global language. Yet inequality persisted in wealth, policing, and opportunity, and movements such as Black Lives Matter, founded in 2013, show that the work of this history continues.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Malcolm X (1925-1965) and the Nation of Islam; the Black Panther Party (founded 1966); Stokely Carmichael popularizing 'Black Power' in 1966; Thurgood Marshall becoming the first Black Supreme Court justice in 1967; Shirley Chisholm, the first Black woman in Congress (1968) and a presidential candidate (1972); and Barack Obama, elected the first Black president in 2008. In culture: Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Charlie Parker, and Miles Davis in jazz; Bessie Smith, Muddy Waters, and B. B. King in blues; Mahalia Jackson and Thomas Dorsey in gospel; and DJ Kool Herc and countless others in hip-hop. In literature: Toni Morrison (Nobel Prize, 1993), Ralph Ellison, James Baldwin, and Maya Angelou. In science: George Washington Carver, Charles Drew, Percy Julian, Katherine Johnson, and Mae Jemison, the first Black woman in space (1992).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What did the Black Power movement emphasize beyond integration? 2) Where and when was the Black Panther Party founded? 3) Name the Black American musical genre born in the 1970s Bronx. 4) Which author won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993? 5) Name one Black scientist or mathematician and their field. Answers: 1) Black self-determination, economic power, and pride. 2) Oakland, California, in 1966. 3) Hip-hop. 4) Toni Morrison. 5) Any one, such as Katherine Johnson (mathematics at NASA), Charles Drew (blood banking and medicine), or George Washington Carver (agricultural science).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: framing Black Power and the Civil Rights Movement as opposites; they overlapped, shared goals, and drew on the same communities, differing mainly in strategy and emphasis. Mistake: treating cultural achievement as separate from the political story; music, literature, and science were ways of claiming dignity and reshaping the nation. Mistake: assuming this history is finished; the struggle for equality and justice continues today. Exit ticket: (a) Who was elected the first Black U.S. president, and in what year? (b) Name one genre of music rooted in Black American communities. Answers: Barack Obama, in 2008; any one of jazz, blues, gospel, or hip-hop. You have completed the course; take the final checkpoint next.

questions.prompt: The constitutional amendment that abolished slavery, ratified in 1865, was the...
questions.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, abolished slavery throughout the United States.

questions.prompt: The 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson decision established which doctrine?
questions.explanation: Plessy upheld 'separate but equal,' providing legal cover for racial segregation until Brown overturned it in 1954.

questions.prompt: During the Great Migration, millions of Black Americans moved from the rural South to...
options: cities in the North, Midwest, and West
questions.explanation: Roughly six million people moved to industrial cities such as Chicago, Detroit, New York, and Los Angeles.

questions.prompt: The Voting Rights Act was signed into law in...
questions.explanation: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned discriminatory practices like literacy tests, following the Selma to Montgomery marches.

questions.prompt: The Black Panther Party was founded in 1966 in which city?
questions.explanation: Huey Newton and Bobby Seale founded the party in Oakland, California, in October 1966.

questions.prompt: Toni Morrison won the Nobel Prize in Literature in...
questions.explanation: Morrison, author of Beloved, became the first Black woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1993.
